title: Pre-production Documents: Mood Boards, Mind Maps & Visualisation Diagrams
description: The purpose of pre-production planning and how mood boards, mind maps and visualisation diagrams are used.
content_html:
Why Plan Before You Create?

Before any media product is made, a creator must plan. Pre-production planning is the stage where ideas are explored, resources are identified and decisions are made about what the final product will look like. Skipping this stage is one of the most common reasons media projects run over time or miss the client's brief. Good pre-production documents act as a roadmap: they keep the creator on track, help communicate ideas to a client or team, and provide evidence that a brief has been understood.

Key Fact

The three main pre-production documents for planning the look and feel of a media product are mood boards, mind maps and visualisation diagrams. Each serves a different purpose: mood boards gather inspiration, mind maps generate and link ideas, and visualisation diagrams plan the layout of a specific product.

Mood Boards

A mood board is a collage of visual references that captures the intended style, colour palette and tone of a product. A designer might include photographs, magazine cuttings, colour swatches, font samples and texture examples. The mood board does not show the layout of the final product — it shows the feeling and aesthetic that the creator is aiming for. For example, a mood board for a charity campaign might use muted greens, handwritten-style fonts and photographs of outdoor spaces to communicate a natural, calm atmosphere.

Mood boards are particularly useful at the very start of a project. They help the creator explore whether an idea will work visually before any time is spent making assets, and they give the client a clear impression of the proposed direction. A client who approves a mood board has, in effect, approved the visual language of the product before a single file has been opened in an editing application. This reduces expensive re-working later in the production process.

A mood board typically contains: images sourced from the internet, magazines or photography; colour swatches showing the planned colour palette; font samples demonstrating the intended typography; texture references (e.g. rough paper, smooth metal); and brief annotations explaining why each element has been chosen. In digital form, a mood board might be assembled in software such as Canva, PowerPoint or Adobe Photoshop. There is no single fixed format — what matters is that the visual references clearly communicate the intended style to someone who has not yet seen any part of the finished product.

Mind Maps

A mind map is used during the idea-generation phase to explore all possible angles of a brief before committing to one direction. The central topic or brief is placed in the middle of the page, and branches radiate outward to show related ideas, sub-topics, themes and potential approaches. Further sub-branches can explore each idea in more detail. Mind maps are non-linear, which means a creator is not forced to think in a straight line — they can jump between ideas and notice unexpected connections.

For a media project, a mind map might branch from a central brief such as “design a poster for a local music festival” into branches covering target audience, possible colour schemes, image styles, text content, competitor examples and potential slogans. The mind map is typically hand-drawn or produced digitally using free tools such as Coggle or MindMeister. It is not a polished document intended for the client — it is a thinking tool used by the creator to ensure the brief has been fully explored before any decisions are locked in.

The key difference is purpose. A mood board is about visual style — it gathers images and colours to communicate how the product will look and feel. A mind map is about ideas — it maps out what the product could contain, how it could be structured and what approaches are possible. A mood board is often shown to a client; a mind map is usually a personal or team planning tool. In practice, a creator might produce a mind map first to generate ideas, then develop the most promising idea into a mood board to communicate the visual direction to a client or teacher.

Visualisation Diagrams

A visualisation diagram is a rough sketch of what the final product will look like. Unlike a mood board, which captures style, a visualisation diagram shows specific layout: where the heading will sit, how large the main image will be, where the body text will appear and what colours will be used in each area. It is produced for static or single-page products such as posters, flyers, magazine pages, DVD covers or single web pages. It is not suitable for moving-image products such as videos or animations — a storyboard is used for those instead.

Key Fact

A visualisation diagram should include: the overall dimensions and orientation of the product; placeholder boxes for images; approximate positions and sizes of all text elements (headings, body copy, slogans); the planned colour scheme; and annotations explaining design choices such as font style or why a particular image will be used. Every element should be labelled.

Visualisation diagrams are typically hand-drawn on A4 or A3 paper, though digital tools can be used. The level of detail should be enough that someone else could pick up the diagram and understand what the finished product is meant to look like. They do not need to be artistically perfect — clear annotation is more important than drawing skill. When submitting coursework for the R093 unit, students must produce pre-production documents including visualisation diagrams as evidence of planning before they begin creating their final product.
exam_tip_html: Exam questions often ask you to ‘explain the purpose’ of a specific pre-production document. Do not confuse mood boards, mind maps and visualisation diagrams. The mood board is about visual style and inspiration; the mind map is about generating and connecting ideas; the visualisation diagram shows the planned layout of a specific product. If a question says ‘suitable for a poster’, the answer is a visualisation diagram — not a storyboard. Storyboards are reserved for moving-image or animated products. Always link the document to both its purpose and the type of product it suits.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pre-production planning documents are produced before any media asset is created; they ensure the brief is understood, ideas are explored and the visual direction is agreed before production begins.
  • Mood boards gather visual inspiration (colour, style, texture, font); mind maps generate and connect ideas around a brief; visualisation diagrams sketch the specific layout and content of a static product.
  • Visualisation diagrams are used for static, single-page products such as posters and magazine pages; moving-image products require a storyboard instead.

glossary_terms.definition: The planning work carried out before production begins, used to organise ideas, assets and timescales.
A collection of images, colours, textures, fonts and other visual references gathered to inspire and communicate the style and tone of a planned media product.
A diagram that places a central topic or brief in the middle and branches outward to show related ideas, sub-topics and connections.
A hand-drawn or digitally created sketch that shows the planned layout, content and design elements of a static or single-page media product, such as a poster, magazine page or website page.

practice_questions.text:
Which pre-production document is best suited to planning the layout of a poster?
A) Mind map
B) Storyboard
C) Visualisation diagram
D) Mood board
State two things that a mood board typically includes.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: images / photographs; colour swatches / colour palette; font samples / typography examples; texture references; brief annotations / notes explaining choices. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why completing pre-production planning documents is important before starting to create a media product.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Simple point (1 mark): e.g. 'it helps you stay on track'. Development (2 marks): e.g. 'pre-production documents such as a visualisation diagram show exactly what the finished product should look like, so the creator does not waste time making assets that do not fit the brief'. Further development or a second distinct reason with applied example (3 marks): e.g. add 'showing a mood board to a client before production starts means any disagreements about style are resolved early, avoiding costly re-working once the product has been partially built'. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what a visualisation diagram is and give one example of a product for which it would be used.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): a rough sketch showing the planned layout of a static media product, including the position of images, text and colour areas, with annotations explaining design choices (2 marks for a clear, developed description covering layout and annotation; 1 mark for a basic statement). Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a visualisation diagram for a film poster showing a large central image placeholder, the film title in a bold font at the top, a tagline below the image and the billing block at the bottom, with colour notes in the margins (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague reference). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A student is creating a promotional campaign for a new youth sports club. Before starting, they have produced only a mind map.

Discuss whether the mind map alone is sufficient pre-production planning for this project, or whether additional documents should also be produced.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering the value of a mind map (helps explore all possible ideas, ensures the brief is fully considered before committing to a direction) alongside its limitations (does not show what the product will look like, does not confirm the visual style with the client, does not demonstrate layout decisions). Argues convincingly that additional documents — a mood board to establish visual style and a visualisation diagram to plan the specific layout — are also needed for a complete pre-production package. Both sides developed with reasoning and applied to the scenario. Secure (3-4 marks): At least two relevant points identified and briefly explained, with some reference to the scenario. Developing (2 marks): One or two points identified but not clearly explained. Emerging (1 mark): A single point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A media student has been given a brief to design a promotional poster for a school play. They are unsure whether to create a mood board or a visualisation diagram first.

Evaluate the relative importance of each pre-production document for this project, and justify which one the student should produce first.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8 marks): A sustained evaluation that clearly explains the purpose of each document (mood board = visual inspiration and style direction; visualisation diagram = specific layout of the poster), applies them to the school play brief, and makes a supported judgement about order. The strongest answers argue that the mood board should come first because agreeing the visual tone (colour palette, style) before committing to a layout avoids having to redraw the visualisation diagram if the style direction changes. Counter-argument acknowledged: a creator confident in the style might go straight to a visualisation diagram. The judgement is substantiated and goes beyond listing. Secure (5-6 marks): Both documents explained with some application to the scenario and an attempt at a reasoned judgement. Developing (3-4 marks): Both documents described but largely surface-level; limited application. Emerging (1-2 marks): One or both documents mentioned with minimal explanation and no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which pre-production document is a collection of images, colours and fonts used to communicate the style and tone of a planned product?
A visualisation diagram is most suitable for planning which type of media product?
A mind map is typically used during the _____ phase of pre-production to explore all possible approaches to a brief.
A visualisation diagram should include labelled placeholders for images, text positions, the planned colour scheme, and _____ explaining design choices.
Match each pre-production document to its primary purpose.
right: Generating and connecting ideas around a brief
Sketching the specific layout of a static product
Gathering visual references to communicate style and tone

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main purpose of pre-production planning?
flashcard_questions.a: Pre-production planning is used to organise ideas, resources and timescales so that the creator is fully prepared before any media asset is made.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a mood board collect to communicate the intended style of a product?
flashcard_questions.a: A mood board collects images, colour swatches, font samples, textures and other visual references to communicate the intended style and tone.

flashcard_questions.q: When is a mood board typically produced in the project timeline?
flashcard_questions.a: At the very start of a project, before any assets are created.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a mind map place in the centre of the diagram?
flashcard_questions.a: The central topic or brief being planned.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference in purpose between a mood board and a mind map?
flashcard_questions.a: A mood board communicates visual style; a mind map generates and connects ideas.

flashcard_questions.q: For which type of product is a visualisation diagram used?
flashcard_questions.a: A visualisation diagram is used for static or single-page products such as posters, flyers and magazine pages, not for moving-image products.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of pre-production document is used instead of a visualisation diagram for a video?
What must a visualisation diagram include alongside the sketch of the layout?
flashcard_questions.a: Annotations explaining design choices such as font style and image selection.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two tools that can be used to create a digital mind map.
flashcard_questions.a: Coggle and MindMeister are two examples.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does approving a mood board reduce re-working later in production?
flashcard_questions.a: It confirms the visual direction with the client before any assets are made.

flashcard_questions.q: Which pre-production document shows where headings, images and body text will appear on a finished poster?
What quality matters most in a visualisation diagram: artistic skill or clear annotation?
